catalog_quote: 2.5 Stress. Stress is not phonemic in Oriya. There are no words which are distinguished by stress alone. The stressed syllable is not very prominent; often all syllables of a word seem to receive the same stress. Roughly speaking, most of the words are stressed on the first syllable: bisyllables: ˈbi rɔ 'warrior', ˈca si 'farmer'; trisyllables ˈo ki lɔ 'lawyer', ˈdɔ rɔ ma 'salary'; tetrasyllables ˈcha pa kha na 'printing press', ˈɔ ḷɔn ka rɔ 'jewelry'. Consider some verb forms: ˈa se 'I come', ˈa si li 'I came', ˈa si chi 'I have come', ˈa si thi li 'I had come'. Some of the exceptions to the rule given above are observed in varying speech style: (i) The verbal ending for 3p -ɔnti is always stressed, e.g. a ˈsɔn ti 'they come', a si ˈchɔn ti 'they have come'. (ii) Complex verb forms can be stressed on their last verbal constituent: de kha ˈjau chi 'it is seen' (see + go), ca li ˈpa re '…

new_statements.quote: To say stress is predictable does not mean it always falls on a particular syllable, as in Polish or Finnish. Chatterji (1926) does describe such a stress pattern (initial syllable of the phrase or breath group) for Standard Bengali, but emphasizes that this generalization does not seem to apply even to other Bengali dialects, let alone a sister language such as Oriya. Regarding the latter, Pattanayak says it is evenly stressed, a characterization sometimes also applied to Marathi (Lambert 1943); stress in these languages is in any case weak. A weak initial stress is also the dominant tendency in Sinhalese and Nepali.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record encodes fixed initial stress (initial stress = first syllable stressed at every word length). Masica does not assign Oriya any stress position: following Pattanayak he calls it evenly stressed with weak stress, and he is careful not to extend Bengali's (phrase-)initial pattern to Oriya. So the type differs (no positional word stress vs. fixed: initial syllable), not merely the position. Confidence is medium only because the page number is inferred from the index and the text was read via search-highlight fragments rather than a page image; the wording itself is verbatim scanned from the item.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Masica gives no placement rule for Oriya. He reports Pattanayak's characterization that Oriya is 'evenly stressed' (no syllable singled out, like Marathi per Lambert 1943) and adds that stress in these languages 'is in any case weak'. The section opens by saying NIA languages are syllable- or mora-timed rather than stress-timed and that stress is generally predictable but not tied to one syllable. Chatterji's phrase-initial stress is stated for Standard Bengali only and explicitly not extended to Oriya; the 'weak initial stress' tendency is attributed to Sinhalese and Nepali, not Oriya.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress for Oriya.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Oriya. (Contrastive stress is noted for Assamese [Goswami 1966] and Siraiki, and complicated syllable-count/weight rules for Hindi, Gujarati, Punjabi etc. — none of this is said of Oriya.)
new_statements.identity_note: Masica speaks of Oriya as a language without naming a dialect; the Pattanayak characterization he relays comes from Pattanayak & Das's Conversational Oriya (standard colloquial Oriya). Majumdar 1970 describes the standard dialect.

readall_conflicts: The one listed work (Masica 1991, p. 121) reports, after Pattanayak, that Oriya is 'evenly stressed' and that stress is weak, with no placement rule — which does not support the catalog's fixed: initial syllable record. Material already held by the project in the same check folder from earlier passes (not in this task's works list, read only for context) splits the same way: Pattanayak & Das 1972, Conversational Oriya, p. 16 says 'In an Oriya word, stress is evenly distributed among the letters' (this is evidently Masica's source), whereas Majumdar 1970, A Historical Phonology of Oriya, pp. 215-218 ('System of stress accent in modern Oriya') gives a weight-sensitive system: initial stress by default in di- and trisyllables with short vowels, stress on a final long vowel in disyllables (kan'a, sun'a, raj'a), shift to a heavy (long-vowel, diphthong or cluster-closed) second syllable (andh'ara, ak'asa), plus double stress in some disyllables; Mahapatra 2007 gives no word-stress statement. So the catalog's initial-stress record agrees only with Majumdar's default case; Masica/Pattanayak deny salient word stress altogether; Majumdar's weight and final-long-vowel rules are recorded nowhere in the catalog.

audit.recode_to: no reclassification yet. If Ray 2003 corroborates Majumdar 1970, reclassify from 'fixed initial, weight-blind' to 'default-initial with weight/quality-sensitive shift to a heavy (ā / diphthong / closed) second syllable within a two-syllable left window; final ā stressed in disyllables; stress weak/non-phonemic'. In any case add Majumdar 1970:214-218 to sources/contra with a caution that the 'weight-blind' element of the primary-stress rule rests on N&P's hedged one-paragraph statement whose examples contain no short-initial + ā-second words.

sources.note: Fullest published account of Oriya word stress (5 pp. of synchronic rules with c. 100 examples by a native-speaker philologist); states weight/quality-sensitivity (2nd-syllable ā/diphthong/closed attracts stress; final ā stressed in disyllables; causative -āi- stressed) that our 'weight-blind initial' the primary-stress rule does not capture; should be entered as a refining/contra source with caution.
